pileated-woodpecker.role: The pileated woodpecker is a keystone ecosystem engineer whose big cavities become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats, and barred owls. It regulates carpenter ant and beetle populations and opens decaying wood to fungi and decomposers. It sits as a secondary consumer and feeds raptors and mustelids.
pileated-woodpecker.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in large dead snags

pine-grosbeak.diet: Buds, seeds, and fruits of conifers and shrubs; some insects in summer
pine-grosbeak.fact: A plump, unhurried finch of the cold high forests, nipping buds and needles.
pine-grosbeak.hint: Plant an aspen and a subalpine fir near a rock pile.
pine-grosbeak.name: Pine Grosbeak
pine-grosbeak.preferredHabitat: Open subalpine spruce, fir, and pine forest near timberline
pine-grosbeak.role: A large, sluggish finch that lives almost entirely on conifer buds, seeds, and fruits, adding insects to feed its young. It helps disperse tree and shrub seeds. Martens, small raptors, and foxes prey on it, especially at nests.
pine-grosbeak.shelter: Concealed cup nest near the trunk of a dense conifer

pine-marten.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects, and berries
pine-marten.fact: Pine martens hunt beneath the winter snowpack through tunnels others can't reach.
pine-marten.hint: Rocky cover and prey near the treeline.
pine-marten.name: Pine Marten
pine-marten.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with rocky cover
pine-marten.role: An agile treeline weasel that hunts voles, squirrels, pikas, and young hares, adding berries and insects in season. It ranges over complex forest and rock, even beneath the snowpack. Great horned owls, eagles, and larger carnivores prey on it.
pine-marten.shelter: Dens in tree cavities, hollow logs, stumps, and rock crevices

porcupine.diet: Strict herbivore: inner bark in winter; buds, twigs, leaves, and mast in warmer months
porcupine.fact: The fisher is one of the only predators able to kill porcupines, flipping them to reach the quill-free belly.
porcupine.hint: Trees to climb and brushy shelter below.
porcupine.name: Porcupine
porcupine.preferredHabitat: Coniferous and mixed forest with trees offering edible bark
porcupine.role: Porcupines are ecosystem engineers whose bark-stripping kills or deforms trees, creating snags for cavity nesters and diversifying forest structure. Their mast feeding competes with deer and squirrels. They are the main prey base for fishers and a supplemental meal for bobcats and bears.
porcupine.shelter: Rock dens, hollow logs, and tree canopies; reuses the same dens seasonally

praying-mantis.diet: Ambush predator eating live insects — bees, grasshoppers, and more
praying-mantis.fact: A praying mantis can swivel its head almost 180 degrees — unique among insects — for a wide field of view.
praying-mantis.hint: Tall grass, a shrub, and an insect hotel give it cover to hunt from.
praying-mantis.name: Praying Mantis
praying-mantis.preferredHabitat: Meadows and shrubby edges with dense vegetation for ambush
praying-mantis.role: A sit-and-wait ambush mesopredator that seizes prey with spined forelegs in a strike faster than a blink. As a generalist it eats grasshoppers, bees, beetles, and other insects, helping regulate insect numbers. It is itself taken by birds, garter snakes, and small owls.
praying-mantis.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; lays eggs in a foam egg case (ootheca)

prothonotary-warbler.diet: Insects and spiders; some snails, fruit, and seeds off-season
prothonotary-warbler.fact: It is one of only two North American warblers that nest in tree cavities.
prothonotary-warbler.hint: Plant a bald cypress with a reed bed and nesting platform.
prothonotary-warbler.name: Prothonotary Warbler
prothonotary-warbler.role: A glowing-gold swamp warbler that gleans insects and spiders over the water. Unusually for a warbler, it nests in cavities, often above standing water.
prothonotary-warbler.shelter: Tree cavities and nest boxes over standing water

ptarmigan.diet: Buds, twigs, leaves, seeds, and flowers; willow is the sole winter food
ptarmigan.fact: It is the only North American bird living entirely above treeline all year.
ptarmigan.hint: Alpine shrubs and quiet nesting cover, with hardy frostflowers in bloom.
ptarmigan.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
ptarmigan.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, wintering in willow basins
ptarmigan.role: A superbly camouflaged alpine grouse that grazes buds, leaves, and seeds, surviving winter almost entirely on willow. It grows feathered 'snowshoes' on its feet each winter. Eagles, foxes, weasels, and martens all hunt it and its chicks.
ptarmigan.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered alpine rocks

purple-shore-crab.diet: Sea lettuce and other green algae, plus occasional carrion
purple-shore-crab.fact: They scrape green algae from rocks and scuttle sideways under stones at low tide.
purple-shore-crab.hint: A tidepool and an oyster bed.
purple-shore-crab.name: Purple Shore Crab
purple-shore-crab.role: A small grazing crab that scrapes algae from intertidal rocks and occasionally scavenges. It is common prey for gulls, anemones, and tidepool fish, moving algal energy up the food web.

raccoon.diet: Opportunistic: crayfish, insects, frogs, fish, small mammals, bird eggs, fruit, and nuts
raccoon.fact: A raccoon's sensitive forepaws carry about four times more touch receptors than its eyes have light receptors.
raccoon.hint: A den log near water to dabble in.
raccoon.name: Raccoon
raccoon.preferredHabitat: Moist forest near water for foraging and dabbling
raccoon.role: Raccoons are adaptable omnivores that regulate crayfish, frogs, and invertebrates while dispersing fruit seeds and preying on bird nests. Their high density makes them a major mid-trophic connector between the aquatic and forest webs. Coyotes, large owls, and bobcats keep them in the mesopredator tier.
raccoon.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows, and structures

rattlesnake.fact: It adds a rattle segment at each shed, but segments break, so you can't count its age.
rattlesnake.hint: Rocky shelter and rodents to hunt.
rattlesnake.name: Western Rattlesnake
rattlesnake.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter near busy rodent trails
rattlesnake.role: A venomous ambush predator and key control on desert rodent populations. It swallows prey whole and eats only every few weeks. Roadrunners, hawks, and coyotes are among its predators.

red-admiral.diet: Adults prefer tree sap, fermenting fruit, and nectar; caterpillars eat nettles
red-admiral.fact: Red admirals are bold and territorial, and will readily land and perch on people who stay still.
red-admiral.hint: Butterfly flowers and wildflowers beside an insect hotel.
red-admiral.name: Red Admiral
red-admiral.preferredHabitat: Flowery clearings and woodland edges near nettle patches
red-admiral.role: A fast, territorial butterfly that feeds mainly on tree sap, fruit, and dung, visiting flowers as a nectar pollinator when preferred foods are scarce; its caterpillars specialize on stinging nettles. Lacking chemical defenses, it relies on camouflage and speed to escape birds and other predators.
red-admiral.shelter: Caterpillars fold nettle leaves into shelters; adults roost on trees

red-fox-forest.diet: Rodents, rabbits, birds, and reptiles; insects, fruit, and carrion
red-fox-forest.fact: Red foxes have around 28 distinct calls, and each individual's voice is recognizable to other foxes.
red-fox-forest.hint: Denning cover and small prey back in the woods.
red-fox-forest.name: Red Fox
red-fox-forest.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and scrub-woodland mixes; avoids dense unbroken forest
red-fox-forest.role: The red fox is a versatile mesopredator that keeps small rodents, rabbits, and ground-nesting birds in check while dispersing seeds through the fruit it eats. It sits below apex predators like bears and bobcats and above the small mammals it hunts. Fox pairs often reuse and expand the same den site across generations.
red-fox-forest.shelter: Earthen dens dug into slopes or taken over from other animals, reused for generations

red-fox-meadow.diet: Voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and insects; also berries and carrion
red-fox-meadow.fact: When 'mousing,' red foxes tend to pounce facing magnetic northeast, apparently using Earth's magnetic field as a rangefinder to judge the leap.
red-fox-meadow.hint: Foxes only return once smaller animals are back, with denning cover and a balanced meadow.
red-fox-meadow.name: Red Fox
red-fox-meadow.preferredHabitat: Meadows, farmland edges, and hedgerows across open country
red-fox-meadow.role: A generalist mesopredator that helps control rodent and rabbit populations, hunting by stalk-and-pounce and rounding out its diet with insects, berries, and carrion. With larger predators like coyotes absent from this roster, it sits near the top of the meadow food web.
red-fox-meadow.shelter: Digs earthen dens or enlarges burrows; uses brush and hollows

red-tailed-hawk.diet: Mostly small mammals (voles, ground squirrels, rabbits); also birds and snakes
red-tailed-hawk.fact: That piercing 'eagle' cry in the movies is almost always actually a Red-tailed Hawk.
red-tailed-hawk.hint: Hawks watch for a meadow already full of small animals.
red-tailed-hawk.name: Red-tailed Hawk
red-tailed-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open country: grasslands, fields, and meadows seen from above
red-tailed-hawk.role: The meadow's apex daytime hunter, soaring on broad wings or watching from a perch for prey below. By preying on voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, and birds it keeps herbivore numbers in check. Adults have essentially no predators in the meadow.
red-tailed-hawk.shelter: Bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge

red-winged-blackbird.diet: Insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
red-winged-blackbird.fact: Male red-winged blackbirds can hide or flash their scarlet shoulder patches at will.
red-winged-blackbird.hint: The thicker the reeds, the better.
red-winged-blackbird.name: Red-winged Blackbird
red-winged-blackbird.preferredHabitat: Dense reed beds and cattail marsh
red-winged-blackbird.role: An abundant, noisy marsh songbird that eats insects and seeds. Males fiercely defend reed-bed territories that may hold a dozen nests.
red-winged-blackbird.shelter: Cup nests woven into standing reeds

river-otter.diet: Fish, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic animals
river-otter.fact: River otters can hold their breath underwater for up to eight minutes while hunting.
river-otter.hint: Otters follow the fish. Restore clean water and den banks first.
river-otter.name: River Otter
river-otter.preferredHabitat: Clean water rich with fish and slow prey
river-otter.role: An agile aquatic mesopredator that patrols channels for fish and crayfish. Otters keep fish and amphibian numbers in check and are a sign of clean, well-connected water.

roadrunner.diet: Lizards, insects, scorpions, and small snakes
roadrunner.fact: It slams large prey against rocks to break the bones, and will kill and eat rattlesnakes.
roadrunner.hint: Open desert, brush, and reptile prey about.
roadrunner.name: Greater Roadrunner
roadrunner.preferredHabitat: Open hunting ground with brushy edges
roadrunner.role: A ground-running predatory bird that sprints down lizards, insects, scorpions, and snakes. It is a key mesopredator on small desert reptiles and arthropods. Coyotes and hawks hunt it.
roadrunner.shelter: Low nests in brush and cactus

rosy-finch.diet: Tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off snowfields
rosy-finch.fact: It nests higher than nearly any other songbird in North America.
rosy-finch.hint: Alpine wildflowers and a rock pile.
rosy-finch.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
rosy-finch.preferredHabitat: Alpine zones above treeline: talus, scree, cliffs, and glaciers
rosy-finch.role: A high-altitude songbird that hops across snow and talus gathering wind-borne seeds and chilled insects. It nests in rock crevices above treeline. Falcons and hawks are its main predators.
rosy-finch.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass tucked into a cliff crack or talus

rough-skinned-newt.diet: Insects, earthworms, slugs, snails, and amphibian and fish eggs
rough-skinned-newt.fact: Its skin holds enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, driving a famous poison arms race with garter snakes.
rough-skinned-newt.hint: A mushroom log and a few flooded water tiles.
rough-skinned-newt.name: Rough-skinned Newt
rough-skinned-newt.preferredHabitat: Pacific conifer forest near still or slow water
rough-skinned-newt.role: The rough-skinned newt is a mid-trophic consumer of insects, worms, and amphibian eggs, shaping wetland invertebrate and amphibian communities. Its potent tetrodotoxin defense drives adaptive evolution in resistant garter snakes, one of biology's best-known coevolutionary arms races. The toxin leaves it nearly free from most other predators.
rough-skinned-newt.shelter: Under rotting logs, rocks, and leaf litter; in ponds during breeding season

sanderling.diet: Small crabs, amphipods, worms, and mollusks
sanderling.fact: Sanderlings chase retreating waves in busy little sprints to grab stranded invertebrates.
sanderling.hint: Two dune-grass plantings and a tidepool.
sanderling.name: Sanderling
sanderling.preferredHabitat: Sandy surf line and wave-washed beach
sanderling.role: A wave-chasing sandpiper that feeds on small crustaceans and worms churned up by the surf. Falcons are a key predator, and its winter flocks track the health of open sandy beaches.
sanderling.shelter: Open beach above the surf line

sandhill-crane.diet: Grains, tubers, insects, and small animals
sandhill-crane.fact: Sandhill cranes mate for life and choose partners through leaping, bowing dances.
sandhill-crane.hint: Cranes need a wide, quiet, well-balanced marsh.
sandhill-crane.name: Sandhill Crane
sandhill-crane.role: A stately omnivore of open marsh that probes for tubers and grain and snaps up insects and small animals. Its presence signals a wide, healthy wetland.
sandhill-crane.shelter: Large ground mounds of marsh plants near standing water

scorpion.diet: Insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates
scorpion.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, and no one is entirely sure why.
scorpion.hint: Rocks to hide beneath by day.
scorpion.name: Desert Scorpion
scorpion.preferredHabitat: Rocky cover with night hunting ground
scorpion.role: The largest scorpion in North America, a nocturnal ambush predator of insects, spiders, and even other scorpions. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods and small prey. Owls, lizards, and roadrunners hunt it.
scorpion.shelter: Burrows and cover under rocks and bark

sea-otter.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, mussels, clams, and other shellfish
sea-otter.fact: Sea otters wrap up in kelp before sleeping so they don't drift away.
sea-otter.hint: Kelp habitat and shellfish beds first; otters follow.
sea-otter.name: Sea Otter
sea-otter.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish
sea-otter.role: A keystone species: by eating sea urchins it stops them overgrazing kelp, letting kelp forests and the life they shelter thrive. It also preys heavily on mussels and clams along the rocky shore.

sea-star.diet: Mussels, barnacles, limpets, chitons, and snails
sea-star.fact: The classic keystone predator: removing it lets mussels overrun the whole shore.
sea-star.hint: Sea stars need established pools with mussels to eat.
sea-star.name: Ochre Sea Star
sea-star.role: The textbook keystone predator of the rocky shore. By eating mussels it sets the mussel bed's lower limit and keeps space open for many other species, maintaining intertidal biodiversity.

sea-turtle.diet: Mostly seagrass and algae as adults; omnivorous when young
sea-turtle.fact: Green sea turtles return to nest on the very beach where they hatched decades earlier.
sea-turtle.hint: An undisturbed nesting beach and clean water.
sea-turtle.name: Green Sea Turtle
sea-turtle.preferredHabitat: Clean shallow water with seagrass and undisturbed beach
sea-turtle.role: The only mostly herbivorous sea turtle; adults graze seagrass and algae, keeping beds healthy, while juveniles start as omnivores. Its nesting success is a strong indicator of clean water and undisturbed beaches.
sea-turtle.shelter: Offshore waters; nests on quiet sand

shorebird.diet: Sand crustaceans, mole crabs, and kelp-fly larvae
shorebird.fact: Snowy plover chicks can run and feed themselves within hours of hatching.
shorebird.hint: Anchored dunes and a protected stretch of quiet beach.
shorebird.name: Snowy Plover
shorebird.preferredHabitat: Undisturbed sandy beaches and dune edges
shorebird.role: A small beach forager that snaps up tiny crustaceans and kelp flies along the tide line. A threatened species and sensitive indicator of quiet, undisturbed beach; its nests fail easily where beaches are busy.
shorebird.shelter: Shallow scrapes hidden on open sand

snapping-turtle.diet: Fish, aquatic plants, carrion, and almost anything it can catch
snapping-turtle.fact: Adult snapping turtles have almost no natural predators and can live for decades.
snapping-turtle.hint: A mud bank beside a lake of 5+ connected water tiles.
snapping-turtle.name: Snapping Turtle
snapping-turtle.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom
snapping-turtle.role: A heavily armored omnivore and scavenger lurking on the pond bottom. As an adult it sits near the top of the wetland food web, eating fish, ducklings, plants, and carrion.

snowmelt-trout.diet: Aquatic and terrestrial insects; larger fish add small fish to the diet
snowmelt-trout.fact: A poor competitor, native cutthroat are displaced by introduced brown and brook trout.
snowmelt-trout.name: Cutthroat Trout
snowmelt-trout.preferredHabitat: Cold, clear, connected snowmelt streams and mountain lakes
snowmelt-trout.role: A cold-water native whose presence signals a clean, healthy mountain stream. It picks off drifting insects and, when large, smaller fish. It is threatened by non-native trout that out-compete and prey on it.
snowmelt-trout.shelter: Cold, clear pools and undercut banks; gravel riffles for spawning

snowshoe-hare.diet: Green plants in summer; buds, twigs, bark, and conifer needles in winter
snowshoe-hare.fact: Its molt from brown to winter white is triggered by day length, not snow.
snowshoe-hare.hint: Cover and forage at the treeline.
snowshoe-hare.name: Snowshoe Hare
snowshoe-hare.preferredHabitat: Brushy thickets and dense understory near open turf
snowshoe-hare.role: A browsing hare of brushy treeline cover whose coat flips brown-to-white with the seasons. Its numbers cycle roughly every ten years, driving predator populations. Martens, foxes, eagles, and owls all hunt it.
snowshoe-hare.shelter: Shallow forms under dense shrubs and conifer cover

snowy-plover.diet: Beach invertebrates: crustaceans, flies, and small mollusks
snowy-plover.fact: Western snowy plovers nest in tiny scrapes right on the open sand.
snowy-plover.hint: Dune grass and a coastal nesting area.
snowy-plover.name: Western Snowy Plover
snowy-plover.preferredHabitat: Quiet sandy dunes and open beach
snowy-plover.role: A threatened beach-nesting plover that feeds on small invertebrates along the sand and tide line. Extremely sensitive to disturbance, it is a flagship indicator of protected, undisturbed dune beaches.

song-sparrow.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds and fruits year-round
song-sparrow.fact: A male Song Sparrow can learn up to about 20 different tunes and sing hundreds of variations of them.
song-sparrow.hint: Shrubs, native grass, and somewhere high to sing from.
song-sparrow.name: Song Sparrow
song-sparrow.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges, weedy fields, and marsh edges with singing perches
song-sparrow.role: A ground-foraging omnivore that switches between insects in the breeding season and seeds/fruit the rest of the year, so it both controls insects and disperses seeds. Its abundance makes it a key prey item for meadow hawks and snakes, linking ground invertebrates to larger predators.
song-sparrow.shelter: Cup nest hidden on the ground or low in shrubs and grass tussocks

spotted-towhee.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds, acorns, and berries in fall and winter
spotted-towhee.fact: The spotted towhee feeds with a two-footed backward hop that flicks leaf litter aside to expose food.
spotted-towhee.hint: A brush pile and shrubs over a bed of leaf litter.
spotted-towhee.name: Spotted Towhee
spotted-towhee.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and chaparral with deep leaf litter
spotted-towhee.role: The spotted towhee is an omnivorous ground forager that bridges the invertebrate and seed layers, eating ground beetles and caterpillars in summer and dispersing seeds in winter. Its ground nesting leaves it vulnerable to foxes, raccoons, and snakes, while hawks and owls take adults. It helps turn over and recycle forest-floor litter.
spotted-towhee.shelter: Dense shrubby thickets and brushy edges; nests on or near the ground

spotted-turtle.diet: Aquatic plants, insects, worms, mollusks, and small invertebrates
spotted-turtle.fact: Each spotted turtle wears a unique pattern of yellow polka dots on its shell.
spotted-turtle.hint: A basking log in a reedy, shallow pool.
spotted-turtle.name: Spotted Turtle
spotted-turtle.role: A small, declining omnivore that forages underwater for plants and invertebrates. It basks on logs and buries in mud when startled.
spotted-turtle.shelter: Basking logs and shallow, muddy-bottomed water

tarantula.fact: A desert tarantula may live 25 years, most of it within a few feet of one burrow.
tarantula.name: Desert Tarantula
tarantula.role: A long-lived, nocturnal ambush predator of insects and other invertebrates from its burrow. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods. Birds, snakes, and the tarantula hawk wasp prey on it.

tidepool-crab.diet: Mostly algae, plus detritus, worms, snails, and carrion
tidepool-crab.fact: Striped shore crabs graze algae but will scavenge and even turn cannibal after molting.
tidepool-crab.hint: Restore the tidepools and the crabs scuttle back first.
tidepool-crab.name: Shore Crab
tidepool-crab.preferredHabitat: Rocky tidepools and intertidal splash zone
tidepool-crab.role: An abundant intertidal grazer-scavenger that keeps rock surfaces clear of algae and recycles carrion. It is a key prey item for gulls, shorebirds, and larger crabs, linking algae to higher predators.

tree-squirrel.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, tree buds, and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
tree-squirrel.fact: Gray squirrels scatter-hoard thousands of nuts each year, and the caches they forget grow into new trees.
tree-squirrel.hint: A nesting tree and fallen logs with seeds to cache.
tree-squirrel.name: Tree Squirrel
tree-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
tree-squirrel.role: Tree squirrels are major seed predators and accidental seed dispersers whose buried, forgotten nuts regenerate the forest canopy. They also spread mycorrhizal fungal spores and occasionally raid bird nests. As abundant prey they feed nearly every forest mesopredator and raptor.
tree-squirrel.shelter: Tree cavity dens and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy

water-strider.diet: Insects and larvae trapped on the water surface; also scavenges
water-strider.fact: Water striders ride the surface on legs coated in thousands of tiny hairs.
water-strider.name: Water Strider
water-strider.role: A surface-skating predator and scavenger that seizes insects trapped in the water film. It is easy prey for fish, frogs, and wading birds.
water-strider.shelter: Still water surfaces among emergent plants

western-meadowlark.diet: Mostly insects in summer (beetles, grasshoppers); seeds and grain in winter
western-meadowlark.fact: The Western Meadowlark's flute-like song is the state bird anthem of six U.S. states.
western-meadowlark.hint: Meadowlarks need real expanses of native grass before they will nest, with a basin to drink and bathe.
western-meadowlark.name: Western Meadowlark
western-meadowlark.preferredHabitat: Wide native grasslands and meadows with song perches
western-meadowlark.role: A grassland omnivore that eats large numbers of grasshoppers, crickets, and beetles in summer while taking seeds in winter, helping keep insect populations in check. As a plump ground bird it is important prey for hawks and mammalian predators of the meadow.
western-meadowlark.shelter: Domed grass nest woven on the ground, often with a covered runway

western-screech-owl.diet: Small mammals and large insects; also small birds and worms
western-screech-owl.fact: This pint-sized owl occasionally takes prey larger than itself, including cottontail rabbits.
western-screech-owl.hint: Plant an oak and craft a hollow log and log shelter.
western-screech-owl.name: Western Screech-Owl
western-screech-owl.preferredHabitat: Wooded edges and brushy areas bordering open meadows
western-screech-owl.role: A small nocturnal mesopredator that sits and waits, then drops onto rodents and insects, gleaning grasshoppers and beetles and snatching voles and mice on the ground. It bridges insect and rodent control in the meadow at night.
western-screech-owl.shelter: Roosts and nests in tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, and boxes

wetland-salamander.diet: Worms, insects, small invertebrates, and even small vertebrates
wetland-salamander.fact: Tiger salamanders are among the largest land salamanders in North America.
wetland-salamander.hint: Quiet breeding pools with soft digging banks.
wetland-salamander.name: Tiger Salamander
wetland-salamander.role: A voracious burrowing carnivore that hunts worms and invertebrates near breeding pools. Larvae grow in fishless water and can even turn cannibal.
wetland-salamander.shelter: Damp burrows near fishless breeding pools

white-crowned-sparrow.diet: Mainly weed and grass seeds, plus caterpillars, beetles, and other insects
white-crowned-sparrow.fact: Young white-crowns learn their song dialect from the neighbours nearby.
white-crowned-sparrow.hint: A heather mat and nest shelf sheltered by krummholz pine.
white-crowned-sparrow.name: White-crowned Sparrow
white-crowned-sparrow.preferredHabitat: Krummholz edges, alpine meadows, and heath with bare ground
white-crowned-sparrow.role: A ground-foraging sparrow of alpine meadow and krummholz edges that eats seeds and summer insects. It disperses seeds and feeds insect larvae to its chicks. Foxes, weasels, and martens hunt the adults and raid its low nests.
white-crowned-sparrow.shelter: Ground or low-shrub cup nest among mosses, lichens, and heath

wood-duck.diet: Acorns, seeds, and aquatic plants; ducklings and spring birds also eat insects and snails
wood-duck.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings leap from nest cavities up to 50 feet high and land unhurt.
wood-duck.hint: A nesting tree beside a flooded pool of 4+ water tiles.
wood-duck.name: Wood Duck
wood-duck.preferredHabitat: Bottomland hardwood and wooded swamps with slow water and cavity trees
wood-duck.role: Wood ducks are omnivorous consumers linking bottomland forest and wetland food webs, dispersing acorn and aquatic-plant seeds and regulating shallow-water invertebrates. As prey they feed great horned owls, mink, raccoons, and snapping turtles. Depending on woodpecker cavities, their abundance signals healthy wooded wetlands.
wood-duck.shelter: Obligate cavity nester in tree holes and nest boxes near water

woodpecker.diet: Mostly insects—beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars—with some berries, seeds, and sap
woodpecker.fact: Downy woodpeckers are small enough to hammer into goldenrod galls for fly larvae that larger woodpeckers can't reach.
woodpecker.hint: Woodpeckers need standing deadwood — keep some snags up.
woodpecker.name: Woodpecker
woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with dead snags full of insects
woodpecker.role: Woodpeckers regulate wood-boring beetles and bark insects, easing pest pressure on trees. Their abandoned cavities house nuthatches, wrens, and flying squirrels, making them ecosystem engineers. They feed hawks, owls, and nest-raiding squirrels and snakes.
woodpecker.shelter: Self-excavated cavities in standing deadwood; roosts in cavities year-round

alpine.description: A trampled alpine slope. The wildflower turf is worn through and the talus is silent.
alpine.name: Graywind Heights
alpine.restorationGoal: Restore alpine turf, snowmelt pools, and rocky shelter for high-country animals.

unlock.label: Restore Redstone Scrubland to 80% health with 15 desert animals back, welcome 65 animals across the whole preserve, and craft an Alpine Restoration Kit.

coastal.description: A scoured stretch of coast where the open ocean breaks along the eastern edge. The dunes have washed out and the tidepools are empty, but sea glass, kelp, coral, and the odd pearl still wash up on the tide.
coastal.name: Pelican Shore
coastal.restorationGoal: Anchor the dunes, restore tidepools and kelp wrack, and reopen the shore to coastal life.

unlock.label: Restore Graywind Heights to 80% health with 17 alpine animals back, welcome 85 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Migration Path Marker.

desert.description: An overgrazed desert flat. Without brush or burrows, the heat keeps everything away.
desert.name: Redstone Scrubland
desert.restorationGoal: Replant cactus and brush, build shade and burrows, and bring the desert back to life.

unlock.label: Restore Rushwater Wetland to 80% health with 13 wetland animals back, welcome 45 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Scrubland Restoration Kit.

forest.description: A logged-over woodland. The big trees are gone, the understory is bare, and the birds have moved on.
forest.name: Old Hollow Forest
forest.restorationGoal: Rebuild the understory, raise nesting trees and deadwood, and welcome the forest animals back.

unlock.label: Restore Willow Meadow to 60% health, welcome 10 meadow animals, and craft a Forest Restoration Kit.

meadow.description: A once-flowering meadow beside your home, now dusty and quiet. Native grasses were stripped away and the pollinators left with them.
meadow.name: Willow Meadow
meadow.restorationGoal: Replant grasses and wildflowers, add water and shelter, and help 10 meadow animals return.

wetland.description: A drained marsh. Old channels are dry, the reeds are gone, and the water that remains is murky.
wetland.name: Rushwater Wetland
wetland.restorationGoal: Restore shallow water, reed beds, and mud banks so wetland life can return.

unlock.label: Restore Old Hollow Forest to 80% health with 10 forest animals back, welcome 25 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Wetland Restoration Kit.

agave-rosette.description: A spiny rosette whose tall bloom feeds desert pollinators.
agave-rosette.name: Agave Rosette

alder-snag.description: A standing dead alder — perch and cavity nest above the water.
alder-snag.name: Alder Snag

effect._default: Bright, sunny days are when most green life does its best work, soaking up sunlight to grow. Pollinators like bees and butterflies are most active in clear, warm weather, and many animals bask to warm up before the day's business begins.
effect.alpine: High in the mountains the thin air filters out less sunlight, so ultraviolet rays grow stronger with every step up in elevation. Alpine life must endure this intense UV while also surviving freeze-thaw cycles, where the ground thaws by day and refreezes by night, constantly churning the soil and challenging plant roots.
effect.coastal: When the tide pulls back on a clear, sunny day, tidepool creatures like barnacles, limpets, and mussels are left exposed to bake in the open air. They face both overheating and drying out, and are specially built to endure the twice-daily swing between being underwater and sun-baked.
effect.desert: Deserts get punishing amounts of sunlight, and with little water or plant cover the bare ground heats fast. Because the dry, cloudless air holds almost no moisture, that heat escapes back to the sky quickly after sunset, so a blistering day can turn into a near-freezing night — one of the desert's signatures.
effect.meadow: Many prairie grasses are sun-lovers, using an extra-efficient form of photosynthesis (called C4) that works best in hot, bright conditions, peaking around 90-95 degrees. The grasses are mostly wind-pollinated, but the wildflowers scattered among them draw busy bees and butterflies on sunny days.

effect._default: Fog is really a cloud resting at ground level, formed when moist air cools until its water vapor condenses into countless tiny floating droplets. For many plants it is a gift of moisture, settling onto leaves and soil even when no rain falls.
effect.coastal: Fog defines many seashores, forming where the ocean's moist air meets cooler air and drifts inland as a marine layer. It brings welcome moisture and shade that ease summer's hot, dry stress — genuine relief for creatures stranded above the water at low tide, who face the greatest danger on cloudless, sun-baked days.
effect.forest: When fog drifts through a forest, the leaves, branches, and the mosses and lichens clinging to them comb tiny droplets from the air. The droplets merge and fall like a slow rain — 'fog drip' — watering the understory, which is why mosses, ferns, and lichens drape so thickly over the trunks.
effect.wetland: A marsh sits under a near-constant blanket of moisture, so on calm, cool nights it readily forms fog and heavy dew as the humid air over the water saturates. This can be a real extra source of water for plants at the water's edge, keeping the wetland damp between rains.

effect._default: During a hot, dry spell, plants lose precious water to the air through their leaves (transpiration, which also cools them like sweating) and may wilt or pause growth to conserve it. Many animals turn crepuscular — active at dawn and dusk — while sheltering in burrows or shade through the scorching midday.
effect.coastal: On hot days, animals exposed at low tide can face air far warmer than the seawater they're used to. Stranded between tides under a strong sun, mussels, limpets, and barnacles risk overheating and drying out, and an extreme heat spell during a midday low tide can trigger die-offs.
effect.desert: Desert life is the master of heat and drought. Cacti store water in fleshy stems, spread shallow roots to grab rain fast, and open their pores only at night to lose less water; a big barrel cactus can last over a year without rain. Some animals enter estivation, a summer version of hibernation, to wait out the worst.
effect.forest: In a heat wave, trees lose water through their leaves faster than their roots can replace it, so they wilt their foliage or close their leaf pores to ration moisture, slowing growth. The deep shade beneath a full canopy offers a cool refuge, often many degrees cooler than open ground.
effect.meadow: Grasslands are built for drought. Deep, dense roots and stored soil moisture let warm-season grasses endure hot, dry summers, and when the moisture runs out they simply go dormant, pausing aboveground growth and pulling resources down to their roots — then spring back when the rains return.
effect.wetland: As a marsh dries down in heat, the shrinking water crowds fish, crayfish, and other prey into shallow pools — easy buffets for wading birds like wood storks and ibises. Many wetlands are meant to rise and fall this way; these flood-and-dry cycles are a healthy part of marsh life.

heat.name: Dry Heat

effect._default: Rain is the great refresher, soaking the soil and waking up roots, seeds, and the countless small lives that depend on moisture. After a good rain many plants green up quickly and decomposition speeds back up, recycling nutrients into the ground.
effect.desert: A desert rain can transform the land almost overnight. Water soaks dormant seeds and triggers bursts of short-lived 'ephemeral' wildflowers, while spadefoot toads, cued by the vibration of falling rain, dig up from underground where they've waited for months. They rush to temporary pools to breed in loud choruses, and because the pools dry fast, their tadpoles race to transform in record time.
effect.forest: Rain brings the forest's quiet recyclers to life. Mushrooms — the fruiting bodies of fungi — pop up after wet weather, while underground a lace-like web of fungal threads spreads through the soil and dead wood, breaking fallen leaves and logs into fertile earth and even linking tree roots into a sharing network.
effect.meadow: Grasslands respond fast to rain, since how much a meadow grows is tightly tied to how much it rains. After a soaking the grasses green up and shoot upward quickly, and the timing of rain through the season shapes how lush the whole meadow becomes.
effect.wetland: A marsh runs on rain, which sets its 'hydroperiod' — the stretch of time the wetland stays wet. That timing largely decides which frogs and salamanders can breed there, since their larvae need the water to last long enough to grow up. A good rainy spell can fill a marsh just long enough for a whole new generation to develop.

A steady rain moves through. The watered ground deepens.
First drops, then a steady patter. The preserve greens a little.
Rain taps across the leaves; the whole preserve smells of wet earth.
A gentle downpour settles in — puddles gather along the paths.

You return to rain-fed soil; the ground recovered while you were away.
Overnight rain left every leaf beaded and bright.

rain.flavor: Steady rain — the ground drinks it in.
rain.name: Rain

effect._default: Autumn is the season of letting go and storing up. Plants senesce, drawing nutrients back into their roots and stems before winter, while many animals migrate or busily gather and cache food for the cold months ahead.
effect.forest: Autumn's blaze of color is active, not just withering: trees pull chlorophyll back out of their leaves, and as the green fades the hidden yellows and oranges shine through while fresh reds are newly made. Many oaks have 'mast years,' dropping huge synchronized acorn crops that squirrels, jays, and chipmunks bury — a good acorn year often decides who survives winter.
effect.meadow: In autumn the grasses turn golden and slip toward dormancy, having scattered their seeds. On the open prairie the wind is a great seed-spreader, carrying lightweight, sometimes plumed or winged seeds far from the parent plant to take root in new ground.

effect._default: Spring brings the 'green wave' of fresh growth sweeping across the land, and with it a flush of waking insects. Migrating birds time their return to this bounty, arriving to breed just as food becomes plentiful, while pollinators emerge to visit the first flowers.
effect.alpine: Spring comes late and slowly to the high country. Deep snow can linger well into the warm season, and as long as it lasts it holds the plants back, delaying green-up — which is why the peaks look wintry while the valleys below have already turned green.
effect.desert: In the desert, spring is the season of the 'superbloom,' when an unusually wet, well-timed winter wakes thousands of dormant seeds that burst into flower at once. The winter rains must be generous enough to carry the plants through blooming; sudden heat or wind can cut the display short.
effect.forest: On the forest floor, 'spring ephemerals' race to grow, bloom, and set seed in the brief window before the trees leaf out and steal the sunlight. Many capture most of their whole year's energy in these few sunny weeks, feeding the first hungry bees before the canopy closes.
effect.meadow: As warmth and rain arrive, the meadow greens up and the earliest wildflowers bloom, drawing out pollinators. Ground-nesting birds like bobolinks and meadowlarks build their nests right in the grass, while emerging insects feed the next generation.
effect.wetland: As snowmelt and rain refill the marsh, frogs and toads emerge to breed in a noisy spring chorus — some species gathering for just a few frantic days. The wet meadows become vital rest stops for waterfowl and shorebirds migrating north.

effect._default: Summer is the season of fullest growth, when long days and warmth push plants to their peak and the landscape brims with life. It is also the season of heat, when plants and animals alike must work to keep cool and hold onto water.
effect.alpine: Above the treeline the growing season is breathtakingly short, so alpine wildflowers must sprout, bloom, and set seed in just a few weeks, many growing as low, dense 'cushions' that hug the ground against the wind. Pikas spend summer gathering grasses into 'haypiles' among the rocks to eat through winter.
effect.coastal: Summer is nesting season on the shore. The threatened western snowy plover nests from about March through September, laying eggs in simple scrapes right on the open sand, camouflaged with shell and driftwood. Because the nests are so easy to step on, many beaches set up protected zones.
effect.desert: In the Sonoran Desert, summer means the monsoon, when afternoon thunderstorms roll in to break the heat. The hard rains revive the parched land but also run off the baked ground into washes that can flood in an instant — the most dramatic season in the desert calendar.
effect.forest: In summer the leafy canopy is fully closed, and the shaded understory may get less than a tenth of the sunlight hitting the treetops. With light so scarce below, understory plants compete hard for what filters through — exactly why the spring wildflowers finished early.
effect.meadow: Summer is the meadow's peak, when grasses grow tallest and set seed and wildflowers reach full bloom. Grasslands are also shaped by fire and wonderfully adapted to it: the growing points of many prairie plants sit safely underground, letting them resprout quickly — often more vigorously — after a burn.

effect._default: Winter pushes life into dormancy and rest. Many animals hibernate or enter torpor, deliberately dropping their body temperature and slowing their metabolism to save energy when food is scarce; true hibernators like ground squirrels can cool dramatically, while bears merely sleep lightly and are easily roused.
effect.alpine: High-mountain animals face winter in different ways. Marmots hibernate deep in their burrows on summer fat, while pikas don't hibernate at all — they stay active beneath the snow on the haypiles they stored, relying on the insulating snowpack against the bitter wind. Both depend on snow, so their numbers rise and fall with each winter's snowfall.
effect.coastal: Winter brings the strongest storms and biggest waves of the year to the coast. They tear loose great rafts of kelp and cast them ashore as wrack, a seasonal feast for sand-dwelling creatures and the shorebirds that eat them, while the heavy surf overturns rocks and refreshes the intertidal community.
effect.forest: Deciduous trees survive winter by dropping their leaves and shutting down photosynthesis, first reclaiming their sugars into trunk and roots; shedding those freeze-vulnerable leaves protects the tree. Evergreen conifers keep waxy needles to limit water loss but mostly pause too, while animals that didn't migrate hibernate or live off autumn's caches.
effect.meadow: In winter the visible grass dies back, but the plants are far from dead. Prairie plants store life in vast root systems reaching as deep as several meters, along with underground crowns. These hidden growing points let the meadow ride out the cold and burst back when warmth returns.
effect.wetland: When winter freezes the marsh into ice, cold-blooded amphibians go dormant. Aquatic frogs settle near the bottom and breathe through their skin, while wood frogs and spring peepers can survive freezing nearly solid by making a natural antifreeze in their cells. Most waterfowl move on once open water grows scarce.

effect._default: A blanket of snow doesn't just cover the land — it insulates it. Deep snow traps heat rising from the soil, creating a hidden, sheltered world at ground level called the subnivean zone, a humid space that stays remarkably steady around 32 degrees even when the air above is bitter. Mice, voles, and shrews stay active down there all winter.
effect.alpine: Mountain snowpack is a natural water tower, storing winter's snow and releasing it slowly as it melts through spring and summer, feeding streams when water is needed most — in the Colorado River Basin, 70-85% of the year's runoff begins as mountain snow. Beneath the deep snow, the insulated subnivean space lets small mammals like pikas survive the cold.
effect.forest: Snow piling on branches adds weight that can bend or snap limbs — a strain called snow load. But on the ground that same snow becomes a cozy blanket, insulating the soil and the roots, seeds, and creatures sheltering beneath it from the deep freeze above.

effect._default: Storms bring wind and heavy rain that knock things down and stir things up — but this disturbance is a natural, even healthy part of how wild places work. Storms reshape the land, clear away the old, and open room for new growth.
effect.alpine: In the mountains, thunderstorms tend to build in the early afternoon, which makes the open ground above the treeline especially dangerous — there's nothing tall to draw the lightning away. Hikers are urged to reach high summits early and head back down before noon.
effect.coastal: Storm waves rip giant kelp off the seafloor and fling it ashore as 'wrack,' which fuels the entire sandy-beach food web — roughly 40% of beach invertebrates depend on it. Beach hoppers and kelp flies feed on the wrack, and they in turn feed shorebirds; on rocky shores those same waves overturn boulders and open fresh space that resets the community.
effect.desert: In the Sonoran Desert, summer's monsoon brings booming afternoon thunderstorms that ease the heat but create its most dangerous weather. Hard rain runs off the sun-baked ground into normally dry creek beds — arroyos, or washes — which can fill with fast, deadly floodwater in under a minute, sometimes while the storm is still miles away.
effect.forest: Wind is the leading cause of 'treefall gaps' — the openings left when a storm topples one or more trees. Each gap lets a sudden burst of sunlight reach the shaded floor, sparking a flush of new seedlings, which keeps the woodland varied in age and full of opportunity.
effect.wetland: Wetlands act like natural sponges. During a big storm a marsh swells, soaking up the rush of rain and floodwater and then releasing it slowly, which lowers the flood peak and protects the land downstream.
